description: We are three students from the Faculty of Mechanics and Mathematics of KNU. We are interested in everything related to algorithms and machine learning.
summary:
Mars Street View lets anyone explore Mars the way they explore Earth: spin the whole planet, fly down into a crater, and stand on the ground where a rover actually stood. NASA's Mars data is rich, but it is spread across many archives with different formats, coordinate frames and height datums, so orbital maps, rover images and sensor tables do not line up out of the box.

We turn them into one consistent model, built in layers. The base is a whole-planet globe: Viking MDIM 2.1 colour imagery draped over MOLA elevation. Around rover sites the plan adds sharper HiRISE terrain. At each Perseverance stop there are 360° panoramas and 3D meshes, placed using the PLACES rover localizations. Overlays come from MEDA weather, Curiosity RAD radiation and THEMIS thermal data. Every layer uses the same Mars-fixed coordinate system and a small file contract, so the layers fit together in a web viewer built on open 3D Tiles.

On top of this, we prototyped AI terrain mapping. A model trained on NASA's AI4Mars labels classifies rover images. Its results are projected onto orbital maps, and a route planner uses them together with slope to plan rover paths.
details:
==================================================

1. HOW IT WORKS

==================================================

Mars Street View combines NASA's orbital and rover data into one model of Mars. The model runs from a whole-planet globe down to 360° ground panoramas at the places where Perseverance stopped.

--------------------------------------------------

1.1 WHAT THE USER SEES

--------------------------------------------------

- The globe. The whole of Mars appears as a 3D globe: Viking MDIM 2.1 colour imagery draped over MOLA elevation. Terrain tiles stream into the browser as you zoom, so only what is on screen is loaded.

- Zooming into a site. Near a rover site such as Jezero crater, sharper terrain replaces the global base: HiRISE imagery at 25 cm per pixel over high-resolution elevation.

- Rover stops. Every place where the rover stopped and took pictures is a point on the map, joined along its drive. Clicking a stop drops you to ground level. You stand where the rover's camera stood and look around in a 360° panorama. That panorama sits on a 3D mesh of the rover's surroundings, so the near ground and the orbital terrain behind it line up. From each stop you can step to the next one along the route.

- Data overlays and panels.

- Thermal inertia from THEMIS, which shows sand versus bedrock from orbit, with values readable on hover.

- Weather at Jezero from MEDA: temperature, pressure, wind, humidity and dust.

- Surface radiation dose at Gale from Curiosity's RAD.

- A terrain-class map (soil, bedrock, sand, big rock).

- Route planning. Pick two points on the map, and the system draws a rover route that avoids steep slopes and difficult terrain (see section 2.2).

--------------------------------------------------

1.2 HOW THE DATA GETS THERE

--------------------------------------------------

Step 1. Fetch only what is needed.

Source data comes straight from NASA and USGS archives: the PDS archives and the USGS planetary data on AWS. It is fetched by site bounding box, and Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs are streamed window by window. Whole archives are never copied; HiRISE alone is over 100 TB.

Step 2. Convert once into open formats.

Each source is converted once into a few open, web-friendly formats:

- rasters (imagery, elevation, thermal): Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF;

- terrain and rover meshes: glTF inside 3D Tiles 1.1;

- panoramas: multi-resolution cubemap tiles;

- rover poses: GeoParquet and GeoJSON;

- weather and radiation series: Parquet and JSON summaries.

Step 3. One coordinate system.

All layers share one Mars-fixed frame: the IAU Mars sphere, with heights in metres above it. Every dataset is converted into this frame once, at ingest. After that, a rover image, the terrain under it and the sensor readings for that spot automatically line up.

Step 4. Independent layers.

The model is built as separate layers, and each is fetched, built, validated and published on its own:

- L1 global globe;

- L2 regional high-resolution terrain;

- L3 rover poses;

- L4 street-view stops (panorama + mesh);

- L5 thermal;

- L6 weather and radiation;

- L7 science overlays;

- L8 web viewer.

Each layer ships a small manifest (layer.json) that lists its coordinate system, bounds, resolution, sources and licence.

Step 5. A street-view stop is one record.

A stop record joins the rover's position and orientation (from the PLACES localizations), its panorama, its 3D mesh, how well the mesh fits the orbital terrain, and links to the next stops. This is what lets the viewer open a panorama in the right place and walk from stop to stop.

Step 6. Reproducible processing.

One container image holds the whole processing toolchain (GDAL, NASA's Ames Stereo Pipeline, Snakemake). It runs in the cloud next to the USGS data. Every published layer is versioned and never overwritten. Its manifest names the exact source files, so anyone can rebuild it from the original NASA data.

Step 7. The viewer.

The web viewer reads only the published manifests and a catalog. It discovers which layers exist, where they are and how to draw them, without knowing how they were built. New sites or datasets plug in as new layers.

==================================================

2. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT

==================================================

The core of our R&D answers one question: what is the ground made of, and where can a rover safely drive? The rover sees the terrain in great detail, but only along its path. Orbiters see everywhere, but at 25 cm per pixel. We built a pipeline that learns terrain classes from rover images, transfers them to orbital imagery, and uses them to plan routes.

--------------------------------------------------

2.1 TERRAIN CLASSIFICATION FROM ROVER IMAGES

--------------------------------------------------

Step 1. Learning terrain classes on the ground.

We trained a SegFormer-B2 semantic segmentation model (ImageNet-pretrained encoder) on NASA/JPL's AI4Mars dataset. AI4Mars has 18,130 Curiosity Navcam images, labelled by citizen scientists into four classes: soil, bedrock, sand and big rock. We evaluated the model on the expert-labelled test split, where three experts agree on every label.

- Class-weighted loss keeps the rare classes (big rock, sand) from being drowned out by soil.

- Strong photometric augmentation (gain, gamma, blur, noise, scale) is there because the target camera is Perseverance's Navcam, not Curiosity's.

Step 2. Transferring to Perseverance.

Perseverance images are resampled to the same angular scale the model was trained on (about 1.6 mrad per pixel) and converted to greyscale. They are then classified in overlapping tiles, and the predictions are mapped back to full resolution. Sky and the rover's own body are masked out.

We calibrated sand detection separately. A bias on the sand score means a pixel counts as sand only when the model is clearly more confident in sand than in soil. We tuned this bias on the expert test set, so the precision/recall trade-off is measured, not guessed.

Step 3. Projecting rover pixels onto the map.

Every Navcam frame comes with its CAHVORE camera model. Rover position and attitude come from the PDS PLACES localizations. For a sparse grid of pixels in each frame, we cast a ray from the camera through the pixel and step along it over the orbital elevation model until it hits the ground. Each hit adds the pixel's class probabilities to a map cell. Hits are weighted by 1/range, so nearby, well-resolved ground counts more than distant ground. We store probabilities, not hard labels, so the decision rule can change later without re-projecting.

The result is an evidence grid: a ground-truth class map of the terrain the rover actually saw, built from thousands of frames.

Step 4. Splitting the orbital image into terrain units.

We split the 25 cm orbital image into regions in two passes. Segment Anything (SAM) outlines distinct objects such as rock plates and boulders. SLIC superpixels (about 40 m² each) fill the remaining texture areas.

Step 5. Describing the terrain with a Mars foundation model.

Each region and each 4 × 4 m patch is described with embeddings from MOMO, a ViT-B/16 foundation model pre-trained on Mars orbital imagery. We compared it with the general-purpose DINOv2.

We found that MOMO's patch tokens strongly encode where a patch sits inside the input crop, which shows up as a grid pattern in the results. We removed this by using overlapping crops, subtracting the mean token at each position inside the crop, and averaging the overlaps.

Step 6. A vector database of labelled terrain.

Regions and patches with enough clear rover evidence become labelled "representatives" in a per-class vector database. Each representative is a normalised 768-dimensional embedding plus its class.

- Rock classes get a lower purity threshold, because even a 4 m patch is rarely pure rock.

- Patch-level representatives turned out to be essential. Averaging over whole regions washed out narrow bedrock outcrops.

Step 7. Classifying the whole map.

For any patch, we take the mean cosine distance to its k = 3 nearest representatives of each class, and the closest class wins. Because every class competes on its own nearest neighbours, rare classes are not outvoted by the common soil class. If even the best class is farther than the database's own typical distances, the patch is "unknown" rather than forced into a class. The gap between the best and second-best class gives a confidence map.

Step 8. Honest validation.

We used leave-one-area-out validation over five Jezero areas: landing site, Séítah, delta front, crater floor and delta flats. Each area is classified with a database built only from the other four areas, that is, on terrain the system has never seen labels for.

- Sand transfers best between areas (recall 0.7–0.9 on the delta and Séítah).

- Patch-level representatives are the only setup in which bedrock and big rocks are recalled at all.

- The weakest point is domain shift: the Curiosity-trained model tends to call Perseverance's light-toned bedrock "soil".

--------------------------------------------------

2.2 TERRAIN-AWARE ROUTE PLANNING

--------------------------------------------------

The user gives two points (longitude, latitude), and the system returns a least-cost rover route that avoids steep slopes and costly terrain.

Step 1. Corridor tiling.

The straight line between the points is widened into a corridor (300 m by default). The corridor is covered by tiles from a fixed global grid of 256 m squares in the site's coordinate system. Only these tiles are processed, never the whole map.

Step 2. Live classification with caching.

For each tile we read only the needed window of the orbital image, streamed from a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF with a 28 m context margin. MOMO embeds it at 0.25 m, and the vector database classifies every 4 × 4 m cell. Each tile is computed once and then cached. The cache key includes the terrain-layer version and a hash of the database, so a new map or a retrained database never reuses stale results.

Step 3. Cost surface.

Slope comes from the elevation model on the same 4 m grid. Each cell gets a cost:

cost = class cost × (1 + (slope / 10°)²)

Class costs: soil 1, bedrock 1.5, sand 3, big rock 8, unknown 2.5.

The quadratic slope term makes steep ground grow expensive quickly. Cells steeper than 25° and cells outside the corridor are blocked. The values reflect rover-driving intuition: sand traps wheels, boulder fields are hazardous, and unknown terrain is treated with caution.

Step 4. Least-cost path.

We search for the cheapest path on the 8-connected grid, so diagonal moves are allowed and weighted by their true length. The route is converted back to longitude/latitude.

Step 5. Outputs.

- A GeoJSON route with its length and the share of each terrain class along it.

- A two-band raster (class and cost) that the viewer drapes over the terrain as a colour overlay.

Example. From the Perseverance landing site to the edge of Séítah, the straight line is 814 m. The planned route is 983 m and bends around the dune fields: 83% soil, 9% bedrock, 3% sand. The first run classifies about a dozen tiles live: about 3.5 minutes when the imagery is streamed over the network, or about 24 s from local files on a laptop GPU. The same route from cache takes 0.2 s, so routes that repeat or overlap are instant.

--------------------------------------------------

2.3 ONE COORDINATE FRAME FOR THE WHOLE PLANET

--------------------------------------------------

For the classification and the routes to sit correctly on the globe, every dataset has to agree on where things are.

- Coordinates. All layers use the IAU Mars sphere (radius 3,396,190 m). MOLA heights are converted from the areoid to the sphere with NASA's Ames Stereo Pipeline. We checked the result against the PDS areoid (mean difference 0.003 m) and measured that putting the MDIM 2.1 imagery on the sphere moves Jezero by 0.3 m.

- Image-to-relief alignment. We measured how well the Viking MDIM 2.1 imagery lines up with the MOLA relief by correlating MDIM brightness with MOLA hillshades lit from 8 sun directions. The offset is about 0.9 km at Jezero and varies by region; this is recorded in the layer metadata.

- Rover poses. The 33,458 PLACES rover poses (88 sites, sols 0–1897) match the mission's MMGIS waypoints to within 1 cm.

- Street-view panoramas. These are placed at the true Navcam eye position (about 1.9 m above the rover origin) rather than the rover's centre, so the view lines up with the terrain behind it.

- 3D terrain. Most 3D terrain tools assume Earth's WGS84 ellipsoid, so we built our own mesher that writes 3D Tiles 1.1. It simplifies the mesh relative to the curved Mars surface, not a flat lon/lat grid. It stores tile-local coordinates, keeping the height error at millimetre level. The whole planet is published as 43,690 tiles that stream into the browser as you zoom.
